passage: "Nine-thirty? Everyone else stays till eleven!" Neelam dropped her bag on the sofa of their Chennai flat. Her mother, Swati, kept chopping onions. "Nine-thirty, and you text when you leave." "You don't even know my friends!" "Then tell me about them." Neelam stomped to her room. Her phone buzzed with plans she didn't share. At ten she came out for water and lingered by the kitchen. Swati was still there, wiping the counter. "Is there any rasam left?" Neelam asked, not looking at her. Swati heated a bowl. They ate in silence. Then Neelam said, "Priyanka's amma also says nine-thirty," and went back to her room, leaving the door half open.

qa.q: What time does Swati want Neelam home by?
qa.a: Nine-thirty, and she wants a text when Neelam leaves.

qa.q: What might Neelam lingering by the kitchen at ten suggest she felt?
qa.a: Despite the argument, she seems uneasy and wants to check that her mother is still there and that things are okay between them.

qa.q: Which of Swati's choices kept the door open after the fight?
qa.a: She held the rule calmly, invited Neelam to tell her about her friends, and quietly heated rasam instead of scoring points.

qa.q: How might Swati have felt when Neelam mentioned Priyanka's amma?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved and quietly amused, taking it as a small peace offering.

grounding: A teenage girl fights her mother over curfew and keeps plans private, but comes back to the kitchen to make sure home still feels safe.

"Where were you till eight?"
"Out."
"Out where, Lakshmi?"
"Ma, I'm sixteen. I don't have to report every step."
"You don't. But you said library, and Meenu's mother saw you at the mall."
"So? Meenu thinks the curfew is ridiculous. Everyone does."
"Everyone isn't your mother." Sangeeta put down the ladle. "I'm not angry you went. I'm upset you lied."
Lakshmi crossed her arms. "If I'd told you, you'd have said no."
"Maybe. Or maybe yes, with a time."
Silence. Lakshmi picked at the table edge. "Are you going to take my phone?"
"No. Are you going to tell me next time?"
A long pause. "If you don't freak out."
"Deal. Now eat, the rice is getting cold."
Later, Lakshmi hovered in the kitchen doorway. "Ma... you're still okay with me, right?"

qa.q: Where did Meenu's mother see Lakshmi?
qa.a: At the mall.

qa.q: What is Lakshmi worried about when she asks, "you're still okay with me, right?"
qa.a: She is worried the fight has hurt her mother's love, and is checking that home is still safe even while she pushes away.

qa.q: What choice did Sangeeta make that could help Lakshmi be honest next time?
qa.a: She didn't take the phone and offered a deal, so telling the truth won't be punished.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel when Lakshmi hovers in the doorway?
qa.a: She may feel moved and reassured that, under the defiance, her daughter still needs her.

grounding: A teenager argues about curfew, follows her friends' views and hides where she went, yet checks that her mother still loves her.

passage: When I was sixteen, I, Nazia, trusted Bidisha's opinion about everything: my hair, my music, whether my parents were "too strict." I argued with Ammi about everything. Curfew. Clothes. Whether I had to come to Khala's for dinner. Ammi told Abbu her daughter had turned into a lawyer. I stopped telling her about school and kept my phone face down. Once I stayed out till ten without telling anyone, just to see what would happen. Ammi was waiting on the steps. She didn't shout. She said, "I was scared, that's all," and went in. That night I couldn't sleep. I stood by her door just to hear her breathing, like I did when I was small. I'm seventeen now. We still argue. But I think I was building something of my own, not knocking her house down.

qa.q: Where was Ammi waiting when Nazia stayed out till ten?
qa.a: On the steps.

qa.q: Why did Nazia stand by Ammi's door that night?
qa.a: She felt guilty and unsettled, and needed to know Ammi was there and all was still safe, as when she was small.

qa.q: What made Ammi's response on the steps so powerful?
qa.a: She didn't shout; saying she was scared let Nazia feel the worry without a fight, which made her reflect.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have seen Nazia's arguments at home?
qa.a: Bidisha may have seen them as normal independence, maybe even encouraged them, without seeing how much Nazia still needed home.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Block B, 14 November. Written by Varun.
Chinmay, fifteen, argued with me for twenty minutes tonight about the Saturday outing curfew. Seven is "for babies", his friends get nine, and he quoted Rustom's opinion three times as if it were law. Last week I also found a second phone in his cupboard that his parents don't know about. He shrugged and said everyone has one.
Yet every Sunday he is first in the queue for the landline to call home. Tonight, after the argument, he hovered by my door and asked, very casually, whether his mother had called about the holiday leave, and whether his dadi's knee was better.
The pushing looks like him building his own voice, not turning away from home.
Next: keep seven o'clock, explain why, talk to his parents about the phone, and invite him to propose a fair rule at the house meeting.

qa.q: What time is the Saturday outing curfew?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's casual question about his mother and Dadi suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels a quiet homesickness and concern for his family, checking on them even while pushing against the rules.

qa.q: What plan does Varun make, and why does it suit Chinmay?
qa.a: Keeping the seven o'clock rule with reasons and inviting him to propose a fair rule, which respects his growing voice without dropping limits.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's parents feel on learning about the second phone?
qa.a: They might feel worried or hurt, since it is part of the life he hides, even though he still calls home every Sunday.

grounding: A warden notes a teenager arguing over curfew, quoting friends and hiding a phone while quietly checking on home, and plans fair limits.

Friday night
Huge fight with Ma about Sunday's trip to the dam with Ritika's group. She said not without an adult. I said she treats me like I'm eight. I told her Ritika's mum lets her go anywhere, and that Ritika's opinion about my life matters more than hers. That was mean. I saw her face. Ritika calls her Urmila Aunty the Warden. Tonight it felt true.
I also didn't tell her about the boy from coaching who walks me to the bus. It's nothing. It's just mine.
But here's the stupid part. At eleven I came out for water and checked, the way I always do, whether she'd left the kitchen light on for me. She had. And a plate of cut guava on the table under a steel cover. Same as always.
I ate it. I'm still going to argue tomorrow.
Sangeeta

qa.q: What was left on the table for Sangeeta?
qa.a: A plate of cut guava under a steel cover.

qa.q: Why does Sangeeta check whether the kitchen light is on?
qa.a: Sangeeta wants to be sure home is still safe and Ma still cares, even after the fight.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do tomorrow instead of repeating the mean line about Ritika's opinion?
qa.a: Sangeeta could apologise for that line and suggest a fair middle path, like an adult joining the trip, while still making a case.

qa.q: What might Ma feel after hearing that Ritika's opinion matters more than hers?
qa.a: She might feel hurt and pushed aside, yet she still left the light on and the guava, showing her care hasn't changed.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows arguing over limits, favouring a friend's opinion and keeping a secret, while quietly checking that home is still safe.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Wednesday.
Ojas (class ten) has been arguing with his parents about coming home late after football, his mother told me at the PTM. In class he has stopped mentioning home entirely and now says "my friends think" before every opinion. He hid his phone when I asked about weekend plans. Today, after the others left, he hung back and asked, very casually, whether I had "talked to his dad" and whether his dad "sounded angry." I said his father sounded worried, not angry, and still asked what time he'd like dinner kept. Ojas nodded and looked relieved. I suggested he and his parents agree a curfew together rather than fight each night. He shrugged, but asked me to send the suggestion home. I've done so.
- Tarun sir

qa.q: What does Ojas now say before every opinion?
qa.a: He says "my friends think" before every opinion.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he asked whether his dad sounded angry?
qa.a: Ojas seemed anxious underneath his casual tone, needing to know home was still safe despite the arguments.

qa.q: Why was suggesting an agreed curfew a good move by Tarun sir?
qa.a: It turns a nightly fight into a shared decision, respecting Ojas's growing independence while keeping family rules.

qa.q: How might Ojas's father see the arguments about coming home late?
qa.a: His father seems worried rather than angry, still keeping dinner for Ojas, which suggests he cares and is unsure how to handle the push.

passage:
11:40 p.m., Saturday
Fought with Amma AGAIN about the 9 p.m. rule. I said everyone else can stay till ten, Yash's parents don't even text him. She said Yash's parents are not my parents. I said some stuff. She said some stuff. I slammed the door.
Honestly, I trust Yash's opinion on clothes, music, even my haircut, way more than hers now. I don't tell her about the group chat or who I like. It's mine.
But here's the embarrassing part. After the fight, I lay here listening to see if she'd still come and switch off the hall light like every night. She did. I heard her pause outside my door. I pretended to be asleep, but my stomach unknotted.
I don't hate her. I just need some of me to be only mine.
- Gopika

qa.a: The rule is 9 p.m.

qa.a: Amma may feel hurt and worried, yet she still keeps her nightly routine, showing she stays steady for Gopika.

Mahima, fifteen, had started arguing about everything in their small town near Nashik: curfew, clothes, which friends she could visit. "Ankita's parents let her stay out till eight!"
Her mother sighed. "We're not Ankita's parents."
Mahima slammed her door. She stopped telling her mother about school. She laughed louder on the phone with friends.
But every night, before sleeping, she walked past her parents' room and glanced in, just to see them there. Once, when her father coughed badly, she brought him water without being asked.
Her mother noticed. She told her husband, "She's pushing. But she still checks we're here."

qa.q: Until what time did Ankita's parents let her stay out?
qa.a: Till eight.

qa.a: It suggests she still needs to feel safe and connected at home, even while pushing for independence.

qa.a: Keep fair rules calmly, stay available, and notice her quiet care, rather than taking the arguments as rejection.

passage:
Yosef, sixteen, lived with his mother in Tel Aviv. Lately, he argued about curfew every weekend, spent every evening with friends and kept his phone locked.
"You care more about your friends' opinions than mine!" his mother said.
"Because they understand me!" Yosef slammed the door.
But when his sister Valentina came home late one night, she found him in the kitchen with their mother, eating leftover soup, telling her about a fight with his friend. She raised her eyebrows. He shrugged.
Later, Valentina asked him, "I thought you hated being home."
"I don't hate it," he said. "I just need my own space. But home's still home."

qa.q: What did Yosef keep locked?
qa.a: He kept his phone locked.

qa.q: What does Yosef's late-night talk with his mother suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he still trusts and needs his mother, feeling safe at home even while pushing for independence.

qa.q: How could Yosef's mother handle the arguments about curfew?
qa.a: Stay calm and fair about rules, keep being available like that night in the kitchen, and not take his push as rejection.

qa.q: How does Valentina see Yosef's behaviour?
qa.a: She's surprised to see him talking with their mother, since she thought he hated being home.

passage:
At the residential school in Ooty, Lavanya, fourteen, was known for arguing with the house mother, Damini Ma'am, about lights-out and phone time. She had started skipping the Sunday calls home, saying she was "busy".
Damini Ma'am noticed, though, that Lavanya always asked on Mondays, "Did my mother call? Is everything okay at home?"
One Sunday, Damini Ma'am said, "Your mother's on the phone. Want to talk?"
Lavanya shrugged. "Fine. Five minutes."
She talked for forty. When she came out, her eyes were a little wet.
"Still busy?" Damini Ma'am asked.
Lavanya rolled her eyes. But she smiled.

qa.q: How long did Lavanya talk to her mother?
qa.a: She talked for forty minutes.

qa.q: What do Lavanya's Monday questions suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: They suggest she still feels attached and wants to know home is safe, even while pulling away.

qa.q: How did Damini Ma'am handle Lavanya's pulling away?
qa.a: She noticed the quiet checking, and gently offered the call without forcing or lecturing.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's mother feel after the forty-minute call?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved and happy to hear her daughter talk so long.

grounding: A teenager at boarding school argues and skips calls home, yet quietly checks that all is well, showing the bond remains.

Dear Mumma (yes, Sarita Tiwari, strictest mother in Lucknow),
I'm writing because when I talk I just shout. Yes, I came home at 9:40 when you said 9. Yes, I said I was at Kritika's when we were actually at the mall food court. I'm sorry about the lie. I'm not sorry for wanting to be out with my friends. They get me in a way that's different from you. That's not an insult. I know I roll my eyes and shut my door and don't tell you things. It's not because I don't love you. I think I'm trying to figure out who I am when you're not in the room. But I still listened for your footsteps last night, to know you weren't too angry. Can we talk about 9:30 instead of 9? I'll text every time.
Vidya

qa.a: At 9:40, when Mumma said 9.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling while listening for Mumma's footsteps?
qa.a: Vidya felt anxious and still attached, wanting to know home was safe and Mumma wasn't too angry.

qa.q: What does Vidya offer to make the curfew fairer?

passage: Okay, you want to know about me and my dad? I'm Reena, fifteen, and lately we fight about everything: my phone, my friends, why I need the door shut. Papa, Uday Sharma, famous for his 8 pm curfew, thinks my friends are a bad influence because they wear ripped jeans. I argue back hard. Last week I told him I trust Ishani more than him, which was mean. And honestly, I don't tell him half of what happens. But here's the weird part. After every fight I go to the kitchen at night for water I don't need, just to walk past his room and hear him snoring. If he's snoring, we're okay. I don't want a different family. I want to be a different me, and I need them there while I figure it out.

Friday: she asked to go to a late movie with friends. Karthik said no. 'Everyone else is going!' She argued for twenty minutes, then stomped off. He heard her crying through the wall. Later she came out for a glass of water and lingered in the kitchen, watching him wash up, saying nothing.
The next Wednesday: Nandini had a bad day; her friends had made weekend plans without her. She didn't tell him what happened. But she sat on the sofa next to him for the whole cricket match, her shoulder just touching his arm.

passage: Sit, Arnab, the Lohri fire is warm enough for one more story. When your Gurpreet uncle was fifteen, I fought with my father every evening. Home by nine? I wanted ten. His opinion of my hair? I cared only what my friends said. I hid my poetry notebook under the mattress and told him nothing. But here is the funny part. Every night, after slamming my door, I would creep out when I thought he was asleep and sit near the kitchen, just to hear him snoring. Just to know he was there. One night he wasn't snoring. He was sitting in the dark. He said nothing about the fight, only, "Tea?" We drank it without a word. I was not leaving my family, Arnab. I was making room for myself inside it.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet hide under the mattress?
qa.a: A poetry notebook.

qa.q: Why did young Gurpreet creep out to hear his father snoring?
qa.a: Even while fighting, he felt unsure and needed quiet reassurance that home was still safe and his father was still there.

qa.q: What choice in the story kept the fights from breaking them apart?
qa.a: The father offered tea in the dark instead of restarting the fight, and young Gurpreet chose to sit and drink it with him.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet's father have felt, sitting in the dark kitchen?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt and worried by the daily fights, yet still wanted to stay close, which is why he offered tea instead of a lecture.
